Resting oxygen consumption in the Southern white-breasted hedgehog (Erinaceus concolor) has been measured in captive individuals under controlled thermal conditions. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded is 347.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 347.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the animals are maintained at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], a value that reflects the species' relatively low metabolic intensity compared to similar-sized eutherian insectivores. This energetic profile aligns with the hedgehog's capacity for seasonal fat accumulation and facultative torpor, mechanisms that allow it to buffer against winter food scarcity. Field records indicate that adult body mass is highly variable across the year, with individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 721 grams [Wwi = 721 grams] during the pre-hibernation fattening phase. This maximum adult mass, documented in populations from the eastern Mediterranean region, represents a substantial increase over the lean summer condition and is consistent with the species' strategy of depositing extensive lipid reserves to sustain prolonged periods of winter inactivity.

Neonatal development in this species begins with the delivery of altricial young that are entirely dependent on maternal care. Newborn pups emerge with a wet weight at birth of approximately 22 grams [Wwb = approximately 22 grams], a modest size that is typical of erinaceid mammals and that necessitates an extended period of maternal investment before the young can achieve thermoregulatory independence. Under the standard thermal regime experienced by gestating females, which corresponds to a core temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the gestation period has been recorded at 35 days [tg = 35 days]. This relatively short intrauterine development time is characteristic of the family and is followed by a pronounced post-natal growth phase during which the neonates more than triple their birth mass within the first few weeks of life. The rapid early gains are supported entirely by lactation, which provides a nutrient-rich milk source that fuels both somatic growth and the deposition of the brown adipose tissue necessary for non-shivering thermogenesis.

The timing of nutritional independence marks a key transition in the life cycle of the Southern white-breasted hedgehog, and it occurs after a defined suckling period. Juveniles cease nursing and begin consuming solid food at approximately 36 days following birth [tx = approximately 36 days following birth] and reach puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, at 213 days after birth [tp = 213 days after birth], both developmental milestones measured under the same maternal thermal environment of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This weaning age coincides with the emergence of the juvenile pelage and the functional development of the digestive system, allowing the young hedgehog to exploit invertebrate prey independently. Post-weaning growth continues steadily, but the attainment of reproductive competence is delayed considerably, reflecting the extended period required to build the skeletal frame and fat reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of reproduction and winter dormancy in this seasonal environment.

Reproductive output in the Southern white-breasted hedgehog is constrained by both litter size and the number of breeding events possible within the active season. Females typically produce litters of 4.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.5 pups per litter] and can complete approximately 1.5 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters each year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate that is achieved during optimal foraging conditions at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The combination of moderate litter size and the capacity for multiple litters per season allows the species to compensate for relatively high juvenile mortality rates in the wild, a demographic pattern common among small mammals occupying unpredictable Mediterranean climates. The timing of these litters is tightly synchronized with peaks in invertebrate prey abundance, ensuring that both lactating females and weaned juveniles have access to sufficient protein for growth and fat deposition before the onset of hibernation in late autumn.

Longevity records for Erinaceus concolor indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] in the wild, a figure that reflects the cumulative risks of predation, disease, and the energetic challenges of repeated hibernation cycles under natu at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]ral conditions. This maximum lifespan, observed for individuals living at an average body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], places the species at the upper end of the longevity range for insectivorous mammals of comparable body mass. The extended maximum lifespan relative to similarly sized rodents may be linked to the hedgehog's lower basal metabolic rate and its seasonal torpor bouts, which likely reduce cumulative oxidative damage over the course of an individual's life. Senescence in this species is believed to be gradual, with older adults showing reduced body condition and lower fecundity in the final breeding season before natural mortality occurs, though detailed longitudinal studies of age-specific survival remain scarce across most of its geographic range.
